extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato and classical/political literature; general educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing works of political/utopian literature (Plato and later imitators), focusing on style, credibility, argument, use of sources, and the coherence and practicability of proposed social ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: unity_of_style
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole work should preserve a single, coherent style; additions from disparate sources can injure unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting passages or thoughts from heterogeneous texts that break the unity of style (example: Bacon's New Atlantis injures its unity by adding Hebrew-scripture material). A unified stylistic manner enhances artistic effect and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: verisimilitude (lifelike_fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictional framing should give the narrator and tale the appearance of eyewitness or factual authority, making the fiction seem lifelike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise dates, facts, and a skilful mix of real and imaginary persons (More's Utopia uses such devices) to make the reader inclined to believe the account; small plausible details (forgotten questions, interrupted conversations) strengthen plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: originality_of_thought
rubrics_metrics.description: A work should leave the impression of an original thinker rather than merely imitating predecessors or producing rhetorical flourishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize novel insights and distinctive synthesis over mere rhetorical skill or slavish imitation (Cicero is noted as lacking the impression of an original thinker despite noble sentiments).

rubrics_metrics.name: dramatic_invention_and_art_of_feigning
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative invention—the ability to invent convincing characters, scenes, and frames—is a key artistic merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a credible narrative persona and use dramatic detail to convince readers (More is praised for his power of feigning; Swift is mentioned as a comparable dramatist).

rubrics_metrics.name: charm_and_beauty_of_style
rubrics_metrics.description: Elegance, charm, and grace of expression are important; some works possess a charm of style that others lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic grace can elevate a work (Utopia, New Atlantis praised) whereas lack of charm reduces its literary merit (Campanella's City of the Sun is said to have 'little or no charm of style').

rubrics_metrics.name: credibility_of_mythic_elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a work employs myth or visionary material, it should make the vision credible or at least present it with an authorial conviction that the reader can accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether the myth is presented as a genuine visionary truth or mere dream; works appear weaker if the author seems not to believe their own creation (Somnium Scipionis is criticized as 'only a dream').

rubrics_metrics.name: integration_of_politics_and_dialectic (method_and_political_discussion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political exposition should be closely connected with dialectical method and methodological enquiry, not merely appended rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interweave discussions of method and political doctrine so that arguments are rigorously examined (the Statesman is noted for interspersing enquiries into principles of Method with politics).

rubrics_metrics.name: treatment_of_law_vs_personal_rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A good political work should address and weigh the comparative advantages of rule by law and rule by a person, and show how they may coexist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge complexities: a person may rule by law, and law can be the living voice of the legislator; avoid simplistic oppositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: critical_rigor_in_use_of_sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should employ historical, mythic, and scriptural sources critically rather than treating them uncritically as facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid accepting myths, oracles, and miracle accounts as indisputable evidence (St. Augustine is reproached for wholly uncritical use of pagan myth and oracles). Be explicit about sources and assess their reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: depth_of_classical_learning_and_language_skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of relevant classical texts and command of language are necessary for persuasive philosophical or political writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A slender knowledge of the literature or poor facility with language weakens a work (Augustine's 'slender knowledge' of Greek is criticized; Cicero cannot mould Latin to the ease of Greek dialogue).

rubrics_metrics.name: quality_of_argument_and_logical_soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments should be logically coherent, avoid false analogies, and not rely on perversions or misapplied quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute a priori assertions, bad analogies, or chopped-together commonplaces for sound argument (Dante's de Monarchia is faulted for such defects). Strive for precise, convincing reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: balance_and_fairness (avoid_polemics)
rubrics_metrics.description: A persuasive work should avoid unbalanced polemics that make the best of one side and worst of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present opposing views fairly and resist rhetorical caricature (Augustine is described as polemical and controversial to his detriment). Balance increases credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: internal_consistency_and_coherence_of_social_policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed social institutions (education, marriage, property, work) must form a coherent, self-consistent system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for inconsistencies or paradoxes in the scheme (Campanella's City of the Sun is criticized for many inconsistencies). Policies should cohere with the broader moral and political aims of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: practical_applicability_vs_ideal_distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the tension between ideals framed by omission/abstraction and their applicability to real life; good writing acknowledges this limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideals should be presented with awareness that they 'require to be viewed at a certain distance' and may fade when approached; indicate which elements are aspirational vs practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: treatment_of_religion_and_religious_tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayals of religion and religious policy should balance conviction with tolerance and practical governance concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sectarian imposition; public practices that do not offend different sects and non-punitive handling of private belief are recommended (More's Utopia provides examples of tolerant arrangements).

rubrics_metrics.name: effectiveness_of_satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire should sharpen critique without undercutting the author's credibility or the plausibility of proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use satirical touches to expose social vice (More's satirical reflections are praised) but ensure satire does not collapse into mere sneer or undermine serious proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: prophetic_insight_and_reform-mindedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Works gain merit when they anticipate plausible reforms and show enlightened social imagination (sanitary reform, education reform, reduced labour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer forward-looking but argued reforms; be prophetic only insofar as proposals remain intelligible and coherent to contemporaries and future readers (More and Campanella show such insight).

rubrics_metrics.name: awareness_of_historical_context_and_authorial_bias
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal or political vision is often shaped by its author's historical circumstances; critical assessment should note such conditioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how much the work is 'bound up with the beliefs and circumstances of his own age' (Dante and More are cited); identify which elements are historically contingent.

rubrics_metrics.name: educational_philosophy_coherence (variety_and_science_emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed educational program should be logically consistent (breadth vs specialization; role of natural science) and plausible in aims and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate a coherent pedagogy (Campanella's emphasis on variety and natural science is noted); avoid utopian claims (e.g., unrealistic scholar output) without supporting mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: conversational_dialogue_vs_oratorical_speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogues should read as genuine conversations among equals rather than as set-piece rhetorical speeches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the give-and-take of dialogue (Plato) to continuous oratorical declamation (Cicero is criticized for making speeches rather than conversing). Natural dialogue better conveys dialectical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_of_figurative_language_and_conceptual_variation
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing high ideals, vary figurative expressions and sometimes employ negative descriptions to avoid becoming enslaved to particular words or metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute one form of expression for another when meditating on higher truths to prevent conceptual stagnation; employ similitudes derived from human qualities but be ready to change them.
